claims.text: Atomic-level chemical heterogeneity governs premelting and melting in Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Chemical heterogeneity locally reduces cohesive energy.
Chemical heterogeneity enhances surface atomic diffusion.
The initially solid Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles are single phase.
Surface effects dominate the thermal response of these nanoparticles at sizes below approximately 50 nm.
Local compositional fluctuations among Fe, Ni, Cr, Co, and Cu produce regions with lower cohesive energy.
The five constituent metals have differing bonding strengths.
Surface regions associated with local chemical inhomogeneity become disordered at lower temperatures than other regions.
Enhanced atomic mobility in chemically heterogeneous surface regions nucleates premelting.
Premelting initiated in chemically heterogeneous surface regions governs the overall melting behavior.
Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles will begin surface disordering earlier than simpler single-metal or binary-metal nanoparticles.
Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles will have a lower effective melting point than simpler single-metal or binary-metal nanoparticles.
Pure Fe or Fe–Ni nanoparticles typically melt more uniformly than the proposed high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Pure Fe or Fe–Ni nanoparticles typically have higher onset temperatures for surface disordering than the proposed high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
The proposed mechanism is limited to particles below 50 nm under inert, stress-free heating without oxidation or contamination.
